slides.say: p and q are prime numbers. Which of the following numbers cannot be p plus q?

So two primes and their sum, and one choice can't be that sum. It looks brutal. Trial and error, splitting fifteen into two primes, then twenty-one, and so on, would take forever. But on this exam there's almost always one simple idea, and once you see it, the answer falls out.

Look at the choices. Every one of them is odd. And remember from the lesson, the primes are all odd except one, two, the only even prime. Odd plus odd is even, like three plus five is eight. Even plus even is even too. Only one even and one odd give an odd sum.
at: Every one of them is odd

slides.say: So if two primes have an odd sum, one of them must be two. Let's take two off each choice, and check whether what's left is a prime.
at: one of them must be two

slides.say: Fifteen is two plus thirteen. Thirteen is a prime, so fifteen works, and choice number one is out.
Twenty-one is two plus nineteen. Nineteen is a prime, so choice number two is out.

Fifty-one is two plus forty-nine. Is forty-nine a prime? It looks like one, but no, forty-nine is seven times seven. And without the two, both primes would be odd, and their sum would be even, not fifty-one. So no pair works, and fifty-one can't be the sum.

In the exam you'd circle it and move on. Here, let's check the last one. Forty-three is two plus forty-one. Forty-one is odd, its digit sum is five, it doesn't end in five, and its root is less than seven. So it's a prime, choice number four is out, and fifty-one, choice number three is our answer.
at: choice number three is our answer
